chunks: "A brushless DC motor is basically a brushed motor inside out.
In a brushed motor the magnets are on the stator and the coils spin, and the brushes and commutator flip the current at the right moment.
In a BLDC the permanent magnets are on the rotor and the coils are fixed in the stator, so there's nothing to carry current to a spinning winding, and no brushes.
The stator usually has three phase windings. If I energise two of them, I create a magnetic field pointing in some direction, and the rotor magnet tries to line up with it.
Before it gets there, I switch to the next pair of phases, so the stator field jumps ahead by 60 electrical degrees and the rotor keeps chasing it.
Six switching states make one electrical revolution. That's six-step, or trapezoidal, commutation. To know when to switch, the controller needs the rotor position.
Most motors have three Hall sensors, 120 electrical degrees apart, that give a 3-bit code telling me which of the six sectors the rotor is in.
Sensorless drives instead watch the back-EMF on the phase that is currently floating and detect its zero-crossing.
So physically it's a three-phase permanent-magnet synchronous machine.

It's called 'DC' because you feed it from a DC supply and an electronic inverter does the commutation, which gives it the same torque-versus-current, speed-versus-voltage behaviour as a brushed DC motor."
